texts.label: section_header
texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We follow twelve synthetic sensors for one hundred days and report how far their readings drift from a fixed reference. Drift is small but steady, and it does not depend on the hour of the day or the order in which the units were installed.
texts.text: We follow twelve synthetic sensors for one hundred days and report how far their readings drift from a fixed reference. Drift is small but steady, and it does not depend on the hour of the day or the order in which the units were installed.

texts.label: section_header
texts.text: 1 Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Sensors that are left in place for months slowly lose their calibration. Field studies have measured this loss for single devices [1] and for small networks [2, 3], but the methods differ so much that their numbers cannot be compared directly. Here we use one protocol for every unit and report the drift in the same unit throughout.
texts.text: Sensors that are left in place for months slowly lose their calibration. Field studies have measured this loss for single devices [1] and for small networks [2, 3], but the methods differ so much that their numbers cannot be compared directly. Here we use one protocol for every unit and report the drift in the same unit throughout.

texts.text: 2 Methods

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Each unit was read every hour against the reference instrument. The relative drift of a unit is the ratio of its accumulated error to the time it has been running, and it is estimated for every unit separately before the units are compared.

texts.text: 3 Results

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All twelve units drifted in the same direction. The spread between units was smaller than the spread reported for networks of the same size [3], and no unit drifted fast enough to need recalibration within the hundred days of the study [5].
